statement: Consider the equation $x^3-x-1=0$. Show that it has exactly one real root $\alpha$, with $1<\alpha<2$. Taking $x_0=1$, use the iteration $x_{n+1}=\sqrt[3]{x_n+1}$ to find $\alpha$ correct to 3 decimal places.
solution:
Let $f(x)=x^3-x-1$. Then $f(1)=-1<0$ and $f(2)=5>0$, so by the intermediate value theorem there is a root in $(1,2)$.

For $x\ge 1$, $f'(x)=3x^2-1>0$, so $f$ is strictly increasing on $[1,2]$; hence there is exactly one real root there (and therefore exactly one real root in total, since a cubic has at most three real roots and the other two, if real, would also have to lie where $f'<0$ \,-\, but on $[1,2]$ $f$ is already strictly increasing and crosses zero once).

Rearranging $x^3=x+1$ gives the fixed-point iteration $x_{n+1}=\sqrt[3]{x_n+1}$. Starting from $x_0=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}
x_1 &= \sqrt[3]{2} \approx 1.259921,\\
x_2 &= \sqrt[3]{2.259921} \approx 1.312,\\
x_3 &\approx 1.322,\\
x_4 &\approx 1.324,\\
x_5 &\approx 1.3247,\\
x_6 &\approx 1.3247.
\end{aligned}$$
The values stabilise, so to 3 decimal places $\alpha \approx 1.325$ (since $1.3247$ rounds to $1.325$).
hints: Check f(1) and f(2); use f'(x)>0 on [1,2] for uniqueness.
Rearrange x^3 = x+1 to get x = cube-root(x+1).
Iterate from x0=1 until the value is stable to 3 d.p.
